title: Secure WordPress Maintenance
description: Run a production-safe maintenance sequence on a live business WordPress site: back up first, update core and plugins, remove risky tools, install a premium plugin from a local package, and lock down file edits from wp-admin.
instructions: You are SSH'd into /var/www/html on production. Order matters — never update before a database backup. Hints describe the action, not the exact command. Type each command in the terminal.

steps.hint: Confirm which WordPress version is running on this site
steps.feedback_wrong: Start by reading the current core version — you need a baseline before any update.
steps.feedback_correct: Baseline recorded. Check whether a core update is available.

steps.hint: Check whether WordPress core has an available update
steps.output:
Available update:
  version: 6.8.3
  update_type: minor
  package_url: https://downloads.wordpress.org/release/wordpress-6.8.3-no-content.zip
steps.feedback_wrong: Do not update blindly — check what core release is available first.
steps.feedback_correct: Update available. Before changing anything — export the database.

steps.hint: Export the database to a dated backup file before any updates
steps.feedback_wrong: Never update production without a database export you can restore from.
steps.feedback_correct: Database backed up. Safe to update WordPress core.

steps.hint: Update WordPress core to the latest available release
steps.output:
Updating to version 6.8.3 (en_US)...
Downloading update from https://downloads.wordpress.org/release/wordpress-6.8.3-no-content.zip...
Unpacking the update...
Success: WordPress updated successfully.
steps.feedback_wrong: Database is backed up — update WordPress core next.
steps.feedback_correct: Core files updated. Apply any pending database schema changes.

steps.hint: Update the database schema so it matches the new core version
steps.output:
Success: WordPress database already at latest db version.
Success: WordPress database upgraded successfully.
steps.feedback_wrong: After wp core update, always run update-db — schema may lag behind the code.
steps.feedback_correct: Schema is current. Review plugins before updating them.

steps.hint: List installed plugins and see which ones have updates
steps.output:

| name             | status   | update    | version |

+------------------+----------+-----------+---------+
steps.feedback_wrong: Inspect the plugin list before updating — know what will change.
steps.feedback_correct: Updates pending. Update all plugins that WP-CLI can fetch from the repository.

steps.hint: Update all plugins that have available updates
steps.output:
Enabling Maintenance mode...
Downloading update from https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin/wpforms-lite.1.9.6.zip...
Plugin updated successfully.
Warning: Download failed for elementor-pro. "Unauthorized"

Error: Only updated 1 of 2 plugins (1 failed).
steps.feedback_wrong: Run a bulk plugin update. Premium plugins may fail — that is expected when the license download is blocked.
steps.feedback_correct: Free plugins updated. Premium failed with Unauthorized — install it from a local package next.

steps.hint: Install the premium plugin from a local zip, replacing the current version and keeping it active
steps.output:
Unpacking the package...
Installing the plugin...
Removing the old version of the plugin...
Plugin updated successfully.
Activating 'elementor-pro'...
Warning: Plugin 'elementor-pro' is already active.
Success: Installed 1 of 1 plugins.
steps.feedback_wrong: Premium updates often cannot be downloaded via the API. Install from a zip on the server with --force --activate.
steps.feedback_correct: Premium plugin replaced from the local package. Deactivate tools that should not run on production.

steps.hint: Deactivate the developer debugging plugin that should not stay on production
steps.output:
Plugin 'query-monitor' deactivated.
Success: Deactivated 1 of 1 plugins.
steps.feedback_wrong: Query Monitor is a development tool. Deactivate it on production after maintenance.
steps.feedback_correct: Dev tooling off. Lock down plugin and theme installs from wp-admin.

steps.hint: Disable plugin and theme file modifications from the WordPress admin
steps.output: Success: Added the constant 'DISALLOW_FILE_MODS' to the 'wp-config.php' file with the raw value 'true'.
steps.feedback_wrong: Block install/update UI in wp-admin so production changes go through WP-CLI only.
steps.feedback_correct: Admin install/update path locked. Export a fresh database backup after the changes.

steps.hint: Export a fresh database backup that reflects the post-maintenance state
steps.feedback_wrong: After successful maintenance, take a new export — the pre-update dump is no longer the current truth.
steps.feedback_correct: Post-maintenance backup saved. Flush the object cache before you finish.

steps.hint: Flush the object cache so visitors do not see stale data after updates
steps.feedback_wrong: Updates can leave stale object-cache entries. Flush before you call the job done.
steps.feedback_correct: Maintenance complete: backed up, updated, hardened, re-backed up, cache cleared.

content.goal: Complete a production-safe WordPress maintenance workflow with WP-CLI: verify core version, back up the database before changes, update core and schema, update plugins, replace a premium plugin from a local zip, deactivate unsafe production tooling, lock down wp-admin file mods, take a post-change backup, and flush cache.

steps.title: 1. Confirm the current core version
paragraphs: Always establish a baseline before maintenance. Knowing the exact core version helps you confirm the update succeeded and makes post-mortems easier if something fails.
wp core version reads the installed WordPress release from the codebase — no admin login required.

steps.title: 2. Check for available core updates
paragraphs: wp core check-update reports whether a newer release exists and what type it is (minor vs major). Checking is not updating — it only informs the next steps.
On production, prefer minor/patch updates unless you have a staged major-upgrade plan.

steps.title: 3. Export the database before any changes
paragraphs: A database export is the minimum rollback tool for WordPress maintenance. If an update breaks the site, you restore from this dump.
Name the file with a date. Keep it outside the public web root when you work on real servers. File archives (tar of wp-content) are complementary — this challenge focuses on the WP-CLI path.

steps.title: 4. Update WordPress core
paragraphs: With a backup in place, update core files. WP-CLI handles download and replacement; maintenance mode is used during the process.
Use --minor in automated pipelines to avoid unexpected major jumps.

steps.title: 5. Update the database schema
paragraphs: Core updates may ship schema changes. wp core update-db applies them. Skip this step and you risk subtle admin or frontend bugs.
Always run update-db after core update, never before.

steps.title: 6. List plugins
paragraphs: wp plugin list shows status, versions, and available updates. Read it before bulk updates so you know which premium or abandoned plugins may need special handling.

steps.title: 7. Update all repository plugins
paragraphs: wp plugin update --all updates everything WordPress.org (or licensed endpoints) can serve. Premium plugins often fail with Unauthorized when the license download cannot be fetched from CLI.
That failure is a signal to install from a verified local package — not to skip the plugin.

steps.title: 8. Install a premium plugin from a local zip
paragraphs: Upload the vendor zip to the server (scp), then install with --force to replace the current copy and --activate to keep the site working.
This is the standard pattern for Elementor Pro, ACF PRO, and similar licensed plugins on production.

steps.title: 9. Deactivate production-unsafe tooling
paragraphs: Development plugins such as Query Monitor should not stay active on live business sites. Deactivate them as part of maintenance.
Reducing attack surface and noise is part of secure operations — not only patching versions.

steps.title: 10. Disallow file mods from wp-admin
paragraphs: DISALLOW_FILE_MODS blocks plugin/theme install and update UI in the dashboard. Production changes then go through SSH and WP-CLI — auditable and harder to abuse after a compromised admin account.
Set it with wp config set so the constant lands in wp-config.php correctly.

steps.title: 11. Export a post-maintenance database backup
paragraphs: The pre-update dump is history. After successful changes, export again so your latest restore point matches the hardened site.
On real servers, also refresh the files archive outside the web root.

steps.title: 12. Flush the object cache
paragraphs: Stale object cache can serve old options, menus, or plugin state after updates. Flush before you declare the job done.
Page cache / CDN may need a separate purge depending on the stack.

troubleshooting: Updating core or plugins before wp db export — you lose a clean rollback if the update fails.
Skipping wp core update-db after wp core update — schema and code versions diverge.
Assuming wp plugin update --all covers premium plugins — licensed downloads often return Unauthorized from CLI.
Leaving Query Monitor (or similar) active on production — leaks debug data and adds unnecessary load.
Relying only on the wp-admin Updates screen — a compromised admin can install malware; DISALLOW_FILE_MODS reduces that path.
Keeping only the pre-update backup — after success you need a new export that reflects the current site.
Forgetting wp cache flush — visitors and admins may still see stale behavior after a successful update.

faq.question: Why is this challenge intermediate if maintenance already exists?
faq.answer: The beginner maintenance case covers the happy path: check, export, update core, update plugins, flush cache. This case adds production security habits: plugin inventory, premium zip installs, deactivating unsafe tooling, locking wp-admin file mods, and a post-change backup.

faq.question: Why does elementor-pro fail with Unauthorized?
faq.answer: Many premium plugins authenticate downloads against the vendor API using a license tied to the site. WP-CLI bulk update may not complete that handshake. Installing a verified zip with wp plugin install … --force --activate is the reliable production pattern.

faq.question: What does DISALLOW_FILE_MODS actually block?
faq.answer: It disables plugin and theme install/update (and related file editing) from the WordPress admin UI. Updates then happen via WP-CLI or controlled deploy pipelines — which is what you want on production business sites.

faq.question: Should I also back up files, not only the database?
faq.answer: Yes on real servers. Use a dated directory outside the web root for tar archives of the site plus wp db export. This interactive challenge focuses on WP-CLI commands; file archives remain part of the full protocol.

faq.question: In which order should I update core and plugins?
faq.answer: Core first, then wp core update-db, then plugins. Plugins often require a minimum WordPress version; updating them against outdated core can cause fatals.

faq.question: Do I need --allow-root?
faq.answer: Only when you run WP-CLI as root (common on some VPS setups). Prefer a dedicated deploy user that owns the site files. This simulator accepts the commands without --allow-root.

seo.title: Secure WordPress Maintenance with WP-CLI — Practice Case
seo.description: Practice production WordPress maintenance in an interactive WP-CLI terminal: wp db export, wp core update, wp core update-db, wp plugin list, wp plugin update --all, premium zip install, deactivate unsafe plugins, DISALLOW_FILE_MODS, post-change backup, wp cache flush.

perfect: You exported the database before any updates — that is the difference between maintenance and gambling.
You handled the premium plugin failure correctly: local zip with --force --activate instead of abandoning the update.
You set DISALLOW_FILE_MODS — production changes now prefer an auditable CLI path.
optimize: On real servers, also archive site files to /home/ubuntu/backups/<site>/<date>/ outside the web root.
Run wp core verify-checksums after core updates on production.
Use wp plugin update --all --dry-run before applying bulk plugin updates.
Document which plugins must stay inactive on production (Query Monitor, staging tools).
